patient.chief_complaint: Repeated 'speech freezes' with headache — three episodes; atrial fibrillation discovered incidentally
patient.hpi:
A 44-year-old American businessman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic after three episodes of transient language difficulty over the past 5 months. He describes his speech suddenly becoming disorganised — he knows what he wants to say but produces wrong words or cannot select words at all. His wife, who was present for two of the three episodes, confirms he produces paraphasic errors and cannot complete sentences but appears to understand what is said to him. Episodes begin gradually over approximately 8-10 minutes, peak, then resolve over another 5-10 minutes. Total duration 15-25 minutes. Following the language difficulty, he develops a severe right-sided throbbing headache lasting 10-16 hours, with nausea and light sensitivity.

Significantly: during the cardiac evaluation following the second episode, his GP performed a 24-hour Holter which unexpectedly revealed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (PAF) — three brief episodes lasting 8-22 minutes. He was immediately started on apixaban 5 mg twice daily and referred to neurology to determine whether his language episodes represent cardioembolic TIA due to AF, or whether the AF is incidental.

He has no prior stroke, no cardiac history, no hypertension. He is overweight (BMI 29). He drinks 12-15 units alcohol/week (heavy drinker). He has a strong family history — mother had migraines with visual aura; father had AF and a stroke at 67. He is a non-smoker. He works 60-hour weeks in a high-stress financial role. He has had occasional 'flickers of light' that lasted a few minutes over the past 3 years that he did not report.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migraine with aphasic aura (G43.1) co-existing with paroxysmal AF (incidental, nocturnal, alcohol-related); AF and aphasic episodes temporally dissociated on ILR

differential.key_features: Confirmed PAF on Holter — real embolic risk; however, ILR shows AF and aphasic episodes are temporally dissociated (AF nocturnal; episodes in sinus rhythm); normal DWI; no LA thrombus on TOE; gradual aphasia onset over 8-10 min inconsistent with embolic TIA
Moderate PFO detected on TOE; however, ILR shows sinus rhythm during all 3 aphasic episodes — no PFO-mediated embolism during these episodes; apixaban covers PFO embolism risk
Gradual 8-10 minute onset inconsistent with seizure propagation; EEG no left temporal epileptiform activity; mother has visual migraine aura — family history of migraine

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI with DWI — exclude acute infarction; TIA vs migraine assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal DWI; non-specific WMH; normal MRA

optimal_actions.action: Implantable loop recorder (ILR) with patient symptom logging — temporal correlation between AF and aphasic episodes is the definitive test
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AF and aphasic episodes temporally dissociated; AF nocturnal; episodes in sinus rhythm

optimal_actions.action: TOE echocardiogram — exclude LA thrombus given confirmed PAF; assess PFO
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No LA thrombus; moderate PFO; covered by apixaban anticoagulation

optimal_actions.action: Counsel on alcohol reduction — primary intervention for AF (REDUCE-AF trial) and migraine trigger reduction; target <7 units/week
optimal_actions.expected_finding: 12-15 units/week → <7 reduces AF recurrence 37% and reduces migraine frequency

optimal_actions.action: Switch ibuprofen to paracetamol/triptan (NSAID contraindicated with apixaban); initiate topiramate preventive
optimal_actions.expected_finding: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk with apixaban; switch acute treatment; prevent migraine with topiramate

critical_actions: ILR temporal correlation is the definitive investigation — temporal dissociation between AF and aphasic episodes is the key diagnostic finding
Continue apixaban for PAF — AF requires anticoagulation regardless of whether it caused the aphasic episodes
Alcohol reduction: addresses both AF (primary trigger) and migraine (contributing trigger); also normalises ALT/GGT
Switch from ibuprofen to paracetamol ± triptan — NSAIDs increase bleeding risk with apixaban
Statin therapy: LDL 142 with AF and borderline hypertension requires statin initiation
contraindicated_actions: Do not stop apixaban — AF requires anticoagulation regardless of neurological diagnosis
Do not prescribe NSAIDs (ibuprofen) for acute migraine in an anticoagulated patient
Do not close PFO — apixaban anticoagulation covers embolism risk; PFO closure provides no additional benefit
key_reasoning_points: The ILR temporal dissociation is the critical finding — AF occurs nocturnally in sinus rhythm-recovery phase; aphasic episodes occur during daytime in sinus rhythm; these are two independent conditions
Gradual 8-10 minute aphasia onset is characteristic of CSD spread from left posterior to perisylvian cortex, not embolic TIA (abrupt onset)
Heavy alcohol (12-15 units/week) is a major modifier — drives nocturnal vagally-mediated AF and lowers migraine threshold; alcohol reduction addresses both conditions
Diagnostic puzzle difficulty: confirmed PAF creates enormous clinical pressure to diagnose all aphasic episodes as TIA; only ILR temporal analysis resolves this

output.query: ILR implantable loop recorder AF temporal correlation TIA migraine aphasic aura dissociation

results.source: Heart; CRYSTAL AF trial; Neurology AF-stroke literature
results.finding: AF detected on prolonged cardiac monitoring may not be the cause of the index TIA/TIA-like event — particularly when temporal correlation is absent. Some patients have both paroxysmal AF and migraine with aura — independent conditions. Nocturnal AF (vagally-mediated) is a distinct phenotype often triggered by alcohol and high vagal tone during sleep. Heavy alcohol use is strongly associated with AF (holiday heart syndrome); reducing alcohol can significantly reduce AF episodes. Growing evidence for shared genetic risk between migraine with aura and AF.
results.evidence_level: CRYSTAL AF trial; ILR studies; observational

output.summary: ILR temporal correlation between detected AF episodes and neurological symptoms is the critical analytical step in distinguishing cardioembolic TIA from migraine with aura in patients with both conditions. Nocturnal vagally-mediated AF is a distinct phenotype often associated with alcohol use and parasympathetic tone during sleep. Shared genetic risk between migraine with aura and AF has been reported.

output.query: alcohol reduction atrial fibrillation REDUCE-AF migraine trigger liver enzymes

results.finding: REDUCE-AF trial (2020): reducing alcohol consumption from >10 units/week reduced AF recurrence by 37% compared with no reduction; alcohol is a potent AF trigger. Alcohol (particularly red wine) is a migraine trigger in ~30% of migraineurs; reduces CSD threshold via histamine, tannins, and vasodilatory effects. GGT/ALT elevation consistent with alcohol-related hepatic stress — alcohol reduction will normalise liver enzymes. Target <7 units/week for cardiovascular health (NICE: <14 units/week for men).

output.summary: Alcohol reduction reduces AF recurrence by 37% (REDUCE-AF trial) and reduces migraine frequency; target <7 units/week; GGT/ALT will normalise

output.query: migraine preventive therapy anticoagulated patient apixaban NSAID interaction topiramate

results.source: BNF; pharmacology interactions database; AAN migraine guidelines
results.finding: Patients on anticoagulants such as apixaban should avoid NSAIDs for acute migraine due to additive bleeding risk; paracetamol and triptans are preferred acute treatment options in anticoagulated patients. Topiramate has no significant pharmacokinetic interaction with apixaban or propranolol; amitriptyline has minimal interaction. Topiramate 25-100 mg/day is a Level A preventive agent and does not interact with apixaban.

output.summary: NSAIDs are generally avoided with anticoagulants (apixaban) due to additive bleeding risk; paracetamol and triptans are preferred acute options in anticoagulated migraine patients; topiramate has no clinically significant interaction with apixaban and is a Level A preventive agent
